name: Angelica gigas (Korean dang-gui)
short: Lab/mouse studies: compounds inhibit platelet clumping; bleeding in people not reported. 12-week trials: no safety changes (extract alone, triglycerides 130-200 mg/dL); mild events (combination, men).
text: In a 12-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 100 Korean people with fasting triglycerides of 130 to 200 mg/dL, Angelica gigas extract capsules produced no significant changes in any safety parameter. In a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial of a combination of Angelica gigas and Astragalus membranaceus in men with lower urinary tract symptoms, ten mild adverse events were reported (gastrointestinal problems, skeletal pain, dermatitis and others; the abstract does not say which group they occurred in), with no severe adverse reactions, and the authors judged them unlikely to be related to the product. In rats, 13 weeks of extract by mouth caused no significant adverse effects up to the highest dose tested, and the extract was not genotoxic in laboratory tests (animal and laboratory data). Laboratory and animal studies suggest an effect on blood clotting: decursin and decursinol angelate from Angelica gigas were as effective as, or 2 to 4 times more inhibitory than, aspirin against platelet aggregation in laboratory tests, and an ethanol extract inhibited human platelet aggregation in the laboratory and reduced thromboembolism in mice, without severe gut bleeding in mice compared with aspirin; the cited abstracts do not report bleeding in people or name an interacting anticoagulant. In a study combining laboratory tests with human enzymes and liver preparations, a single-dose pharmacokinetic study in healthy people and a mouse experiment, the authors suggest that the liver enzymes CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 may play a crucial role in breaking down decursinol angelate and, to a lesser extent, decursin (which esterases can also break down), and say that interactions with CYP-inhibiting drugs should be considered in future studies.
